evidence.quote: Ferries shuttled people across the Yadkin River at Rockford until 1900, when piano-seller R.F. Bland charged a quarter to cross a bridge he built

evidence.quote: near Mount Airy

evidence.claim: Round Peak names both a community and a style of old-time music practiced in the area.

evidence.quote: The community of Round Peak is named for the nearby summit of Round Peak which has an elevation of 2,094 feet

evidence.claim: The musical tradition draws on Anglo-Celtic fiddle and African banjo music.
evidence.quote: Round Peak style is one variation of music drawing on Anglo-Celtic fiddle and African banjo music

evidence.claim: Its banjo playing uses syncopated drop-thumb rhythms and melodic noting.
evidence.quote: incorporating banjo "with syncopated rhythms made by drop thumbs and the melodic nature of noting."

evidence.claim: Research materials on the style are held in Appalachian State University’s W. L. Eury Appalachian Collection, and the area hosts the Mount Airy Fiddlers Convention.
evidence.quote: The area hosts the Mount Airy Fiddlers Convention and the W. L. Eury Appalachian Collection at Appalachian State University houses research materials on Round Peak old time music.

evidence.quote: Big Pinnacle (also called "The Knob") has high and colorful bare rock walls, with a rounded top covered by vegetation

evidence.claim: The mountain reaches 2,421 feet above sea level, with Big Pinnacle and Little Pinnacle forming its two distinctive features.
evidence.quote: Pilot Mountain, a monadnock rising to a peak 2,421 feet (738 m) above sea level

evidence.claim: Big Pinnacle and Little Pinnacle forming its two distinctive features
evidence.quote: Pilot Mountain has two distinctive features, named Big Pinnacle and Little Pinnacle.

evidence.claim: Pilot Mountain is a remnant of the ancient Sauratown Mountains.
evidence.quote: It is a remnant of the ancient chain of Sauratown Mountains.

evidence.claim: As the mountain eroded, its resistant quartzite core remained, forming Big Pinnacle.
evidence.quote: As the mountain eroded away, the solid core of quartzite remained stable, resulting in Big Pinnacle

evidence.claim: Little Pinnacle has a different composition: biotite gneiss layered with schist.
evidence.quote: Little Pinnacle is made of biotite gneiss, compositely layered with schist.

evidence.claim: A curved depression separates the ridge slope, Little Pinnacle and Big Pinnacle’s rounded knob.
evidence.quote: The curved depression between the ridge slope, the Little Pinnacle, and the round knob of the Big Pinnacle enhances the mountain's distinctive appearance from a distance.

evidence.claim: Pilot Mountain State Park extends to the Yadkin River through a corridor of land.
evidence.quote: Pilot Mountain is part of Pilot Mountain State Park, which extends to the Yadkin River via a corridor of land

evidence.claim: Look for Big Pinnacle’s bare walls and rounded, vegetation-covered top.

evidence.claim: The town was founded in 1790 to serve as Surry’s county seat after Stokes County was split off.
evidence.quote: Rockford was founded in 1790 to be the county seat of Surry after Surry was split to form Stokes County

evidence.claim: The former county courthouse survives from Rockford’s years as the Surry County seat.
evidence.quote: Several notable historical structures from the village's period as county seat are still standing, including the former county courthouse.

evidence.claim: Beside the river, the former Southern Railway line is now used by the Yadkin Valley Railroad.
evidence.quote: Rockford sits along the former Southern Railway, now used by the Yadkin Valley Railroad

flags: Partial overview: cache 00 is a truncated DOT guide ending at Historic Flat Rock, not the Yadkin chapter indicated by its URL fragment. Contents confirm the named byway only. Mileage (76.5), two-hour drive, alignment, designation rationale and construction history are unavailable.

Dropped current claims of tobacco being replaced by vineyards and Pilot Mountain remaining visible for much of the drive; surviving pages establish tobacco farming and vineyards separately, not that transition or route-wide sightline.

Geographic itinerary follows material’s strip towns as context, without claiming verified connecting road numbers. Pilot Mountain is retained with exact title and coordinates as a separate excursion before Rockford; cache does not establish a roadside viewpoint or detour mileage.

Rockford bridge builder is R.F. Bland in the history section but J.F. Bland in attractions; R.F. retained for the dated bridge narrative, discrepancy unresolved. County-seat transfer dates also differ (1851/1853); dates omitted.
No named-musician performance or present visitor access promised. Geological description relies on the sole supplied Pilot Mountain source.
